In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them.

After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong.

pg:https://time.com/article/2026/11/09/t.desc: The fourth annual TIME100 Climate list of 2026 identifies 100 leaders driving measurable, successful, and equitable business climate action.
paras: Sometimes you need to climb 30 ft. in the air, atop a modified oil rig, to get a better view of what’s coming next. In October, TIME’s Justin Worland did just that when he traveled to southwestern Utah, where Fervo Energy is adopting fossil-fuel technologies for a rapidly changing energy landscape.

When we launched TIME100 Climate in 2023, funding from the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act, the single largest climate investment in American history, was starting to flow through the U.S. economy, making the country an exemplar of how government policy can influence climate action. Three years later, we’re in a very different world—with signals that new investment is being driven less by direction from Washington than by desire from markets.

In May, Fervo Energy staged one of the largest U.S. clean-energy initial public offerings in history. This was fueled by the geothermal-energy company’s Cape Station plant in Utah, with 100 MW of power scheduled by the end of 2026 and an additional 400 MW planned in 2028—which would be enough to power 500,000 homes. In September, Google signed a landmark deal for the plant to supply power to a future data center in the area.

pg:https://time.com/collection/time100-c.desc: Find out why Bill Frist is on TIME's 2026 list of the 100 most influential leaders driving business climate action.
paras: Dr. Bill Frist is a heart and lung surgeon, former U.S. Senate majority leader, and Chair of the Global Board of Directors for The Nature Conservancy nonprofit. He has emerged as a prominent Republican advocate for climate action, seeking to bridge the partisan divide by emphasizing how protecting the environment benefits human health. Earlier this year, he was interviewed on stage by former Vice President Al Gore, telling the audience that climate change is the “number one force multiplier” in many public health problems.

I believe the single most important action next year is to dramatically scale new financing mechanisms already bringing billions of dollars into conservation and climate action. As The Nature Conservancy's Global Board Chair, I have watched two recently developed tools move from experiment to proof. First, Nature Bonds, which TNC helped pioneer, allow countries to refinance sovereign debt on significantly better terms and direct the savings into long-term conservation. Six projects are expected to unlock approximately $1 billion.

Second, Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) uniquely brings governments, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, philanthropy, and private capital into a single overarching agreement, tying certain funding commitments to community benefits, measurable outcomes, and accountability. Through Enduring Earth, PFPs have secured more than $2 billion in sustainable financing while supporting durable conservation across 245 million hectares.

pg:https://time.com/collection/time100-c.desc: Find out why Xavier Laguarta Soler is on TIME's 2026 list of the 100 most influential leaders driving business climate action.
paras: What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government, needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?More governments need to stop debating carbon markets and start using them. Look at aviation: Under the United Nations’ aviation climate scheme, airlines must buy roughly 200 million carbon credits to offset the growth in their emissions through 2026. Only about 10 countries have authorized projects to sell to them. That's money meant for climate projects in developing countries, waiting on a government signature.

Voluntary buying by companies got these markets started, but it will never be big enough on its own. Singapore and Japan are great case studies. Both now put a price on carbon for their largest emitters and let them cover part of the bill with credits from projects abroad. Singapore alone has signed carbon agreements with a dozen countries. More governments should follow, both by pricing carbon at home and by authorizing projects that can sell to these buyers.

What is a climate solution that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?In India, more than half the nitrogen farmers spread on their fields is never taken up by the crop. Some washes into groundwater. Some escapes into the air as nitrous oxide, a gas about 270 times more potent than carbon dioxide that has driven roughly a tenth of global warming so far.

paras: Today is the Cop31 leaders’ summit in Antalya, where world leaders are supposed to appear, hear each others’ concerns and pledge their commitment to solving the climate crisis.

But attendance is looking a little thin. Germany, France, Italy, Denmark, Ireland, Netherlands, Canada, and Japan are among those countries whose leaders have chosen not to make an appearance. That is a heavyweight non-lineup. It means the UK will be the only member of the G7 whose leader has bothered to show.

Photo: Reuters World leaders are set to begin formal discussions today (11 November) at the United Nations climate change conference in Turkey, seeking concrete measures to tackle global warming amid growing concerns that efforts to address the crisis remain inadequate and too slow.

However, the extent of progress that can be achieved at the Conference of the Parties, known as COP31, remains uncertain, with previous climate summits facing criticism over unfulfilled commitments and limited results.

At the 2023 conference in Dubai, delegates agreed to move away from fossil fuels, including coal, oil and gas, which are the main drivers of climate change. But subsequent conferences in Azerbaijan and Brazil failed to reach significant agreements on emissions reductions.
